# Early Mobilization in a Pediatric Intensive Care Unit: A Qualitative Sustainability Analysis of PICU Up!

**Authors:** Ruchit V. Patel; Juliana Redivo; Archana Nelliot; Michelle N. Eakin; Beth Wieczorek; Julie Quinn; Ayse P. Gurses; Michele C. Balas; Dale M. Needham; Sapna R. Kudchadkar

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Anesthesiology and Critical Care Medicine, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, Maryland. | 2Department of Pediatrics, Penn State Health Milton S. Hershey Medical Center, Hershey, Pennsylvania. | 3Department of Medicine, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, Maryland. | 4Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, Maryland. | 5Department of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, Maryland. | 6Armstrong Institute for Patient Safety and Quality, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, Maryland. | 7Center for Healthy Aging, Self-Management, and Complex Care, College of Nursing, The Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio. | 8Department of Pediatrics, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, Maryland.

## Abstract

To identify staff-reported factors and perceptions that influenced implementation and sustainability of an early mobilization program (PICU Up!) in the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU).

A qualitative study using semi-structured phone interviews to characterize interprofessional staff perspectives of the PICU Up! program. Following data saturation, thematic analysis was performed on interview transcripts.

Tertiary-care PICU in the Johns Hopkins Hospital, Baltimore, MD, USA (JHH).

Interprofessional PICU staff.

None.

Fifty-two staff members involved in PICU mobilization across multiple disciplines were interviewed. Three constructs emerged that reflected the different stages of PICU Up! program execution: 1) Factors Influencing the Implementation Process, 2) Staff Perceptions of PICU Up!, and 3) Improvements in Program Integration. Themes were developed within these constructs, addressing facilitators for PICU Up! implementation, cultural changes for unit-wide integration, positive impressions toward early mobility, barriers to program sustainability, and refinements for more robust staff and family engagement.

Three years after implementation, PICU Up! remains well-received by staff, positively influencing role satisfaction and PICU team dynamics. Further, patients and family members are perceived to be enthusiastic about mobility efforts, driving staff support. Through an ongoing focus on stakeholder buy-in, interprofessional engagement, and bundled care to promote mobility, the program has become part of the culture in the JHH PICU. However, several barriers remain that prevent consistent execution of early mobility, including challenges with resource management, sedation decisions, and patient heterogeneity. Characterizing these staff perceptions can facilitate the development of solutions that use institutional strengths to grow and sustain PICU mobility initiatives.

## INTRODUCTION

Critically ill children face numerous challenges as a result of pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission, including acquired weakness, sleep disruption, and delirium (1–3). After hospital discharge, children continue to experience persistent physical, cognitive, and behavioral changes that negatively impact recovery (4–8). Evidence from the adult intensive care unit (ICU), where similar post-ICU issues are prevalent, clearly demonstrates that early mobilization can decrease these complications while also reducing hospital length of stay, improving motor function, and decreasing time on mechanical ventilation (9–13). The potential negative impact of a PICU admission on functional outcomes has raised interest in incorporating early mobilization as part of the PICU care plan (14–16). “PICU Up!” at the Johns Hopkins Hospital (JHH) was the first structured, interprofessional, early mobilization program shown to increase the activity of children in a tertiary-care PICU (17). The initial quality improvement initiative – with emphasis on a multicomponent bundled approach to sleep hygiene and delirium prevention – showed that PICU Up! was safe with no adverse events.

Despite expanding literature supporting the feasibility of early mobilization initiatives, the resource-intensive nature of mobility, heterogeneity of PICU patients, and lack of provider comfort in mobilizing critically ill patients have hindered widespread adoption (15, 18–23). Therefore, it is imperative to understand how interprofessional staff perspectives surrounding these challenges influence sustainability of PICU mobilization program components. As early mobility is part of the larger ICU liberation ABCDEF bundle (Assess, prevent, and manage pain; Both spontaneous awakening and breathing trials; Choice of analgesia and sedation; Delirium prevention; Early mobility; Family empowerment), it is also critical to determine how early mobility integrates with other bundle criteria in the PICU (24). The objective of this qualitative assessment was to identify staff reported factors that influenced PICU Up! implementation as well as the perceived facilitators and barriers that continue to affect the sustainability of this early mobility initiative.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Setting and Participants

Staff in the JHH PICU involved in facilitating early mobilization, including those who designed and implemented the PICU Up! program in 2015, were invited to participate via email invitation. After collecting contact information and availability, purposive sampling was used to capture perspectives across disciplines engaged administratively or clinically with PICU Up!. Participants were interviewed from February 2018 through August 2018 and the Johns Hopkins Institutional Review Board acknowledged this as a quality improvement project.

### Interview Process

Participants shared demographic information before the start of a semi-structured telephone interview. One trained male research staff member independent of the JHH PICU (RVP) conducted the interviews using a written guide constructed through recommendations from faculty and staff who had experience with PICU rehabilitation, qualitative methods, and implementation science (Supplemental Digital Content 1). All participants were notified of the interviewer’s independence from the JHH PICU. The interviews were audiotaped and transcribed verbatim (including non-verbal cues) by research staff for data analysis. After each interview, investigators (RVP, SRK) reviewed transcripts to determine which themes required further exploration and adapted the interview guide iteratively (25). No repeat interviews were performed, and data were collected until saturation: the point at which informational redundancy was met with at least three transcripts. The COREQ checklist of qualitative research reporting criteria was followed (Supplemental Digital Content 2).

### Data Analysis

Through a thematic review of interview transcripts, a team of four investigators (RVP, JR, AN, SRK) developed an initial codebook (26). Two independent raters (RVP, JR) inductively coded the transcripts using the Dedoose online application (Version 8.2.14, SocioCultural Research Consultants LLC, 2019, Los Angeles, CA) by applying the codebook to each transcript. The principal investigator (SRK), involved in the development of PICU Up!, resolved discrepancies. Consensus among all three was established to ensure consistency and reproducibility of results. Any emerging codes during data analysis were added to the codebook once both independent raters were in agreement. Thematic analysis was used to categorize the reported perceptions of PICU Up! as well as unit-level facilitators, barriers, and cultural changes impacting PICU Up! sustainability.

## RESULTS

Fifty-two staff members with a median of 5.25 years of experience working in the JHH PICU (interquartile range: 2 – 9.25) participated in individual semi-structured interviews. The following disciplines were represented: nursing (RN), nurse practitioners (NP), intensivists (MD, including PICU fellows and attending physicians), respiratory therapy (RT), physical therapy (PT), occupational therapy (OT), speech-language pathology (SLP), child life (specialists who help patients and families cope with the impact of illness) (27), and social work (SW). Demographic data for participants are reported in Table 1. The mean interview duration (± standard deviation) was 33 ± 10 minutes, and coders demonstrated high agreement before thematic analysis and consolidation (mean percent agreement at initial coding: 88%).

Analysis of coded interview data revealed three broad constructs connected to the PICU Up! program: 1) Factors Influencing the Implementation Process, 2) Staff Perceptions of PICU Up!, and 3) Improvements in Program Integration. Themes identified within these constructs addressed facilitators, barriers, and cultural changes that influenced the sustainability of PICU early mobility (Figure 1). Additional quotes from the interview data contextualizing these constructs and themes can be found in Figure 2. All quotes that follow, as well as those in Figure 2, were collected from distinct participants.

### Factors Influencing the Implementation Process

Two distinct factors focused on the PICU Up! implementation process: 1) Cultural and Procedural Changes and 2) PICU Up! Implementation Facilitators. These factors included several themes that impacted implementation success and unit engagement with the PICU Up! program.

#### Cultural and Procedural Changes

#### Normalization of Patient Routines.

The introduction of a mobility routine was perceived to be a strong contributor to establishing a sense of normalcy for patients and family members. RN, NP, PT, OT, and child life participants recounted mobilization periods that incorporated activities families would perform at home, such as sharing a meal with their child. Mobility was described as a vital piece to create a more comfortable environment, helping families cope in the hospital. “We’re letting kids be kids in a more meaningful way than I think really sick children were treated prior [to PICU Up!].”– Child life

#### Setting Sedation Goals.

Participants stressed the importance of setting sedation goals daily during rounds to achieve a child’s mobility targets. Sedation goals included a shift away from using opioids and benzodiazepines while safely weaning patients at earlier time points. Validated tools such as the State Behavioral Scale (SBS) helped staff have metric-driven conversations regarding a patient’s current and future sedation status. This enabled RNs, PTs, and OTs to successfully plan mobility activities.

#### Increased Attention to Delirium.

Routine delirium screening – a component of the ABCDEF bundle – was a building block of the PICU Up! program. According to participants who worked in the JHH PICU before PICU Up! implementation, assessments for delirium were historically not prioritized. However, after PICU Up! implementation, the discussion surrounding delirium increased, with staff perceiving an association between mobilization and delirium prevention. RNs, NPs, and MDs stated that the focus on delirium has highlighted the need for ongoing improvement in delirium screening practices.

#### Greater Focus on Sleep Hygiene.

Promotion of healthy sleep habits, or sleep hygiene, was another integral component of the PICU Up! program. Participants described how PICU Up! increased attention to PICU practices that often interfere with sleep routines. RNs and NPs emphasized the push to personalize patient schedules and plan interventions such as baths and weights to minimize sleep disturbances. While promotion of sleep hygiene was generally perceived as a work in progress, most participants highlighted a link between PICU Up! mobilization activities and sleep patterns. Physical activity throughout the day was believed to set a normalized routine, helping patients establish and maintain a day-night cycle. “I think – just like anybody else – getting up and active during the day promotes sleep at night.”– RN

#### PICU Up! Implementation Facilitators

#### Interprofessional Team of Champions.

Strong representative leadership in the planning and deployment of PICU Up! was essential. Interprofessional champions ensured individuals from every PICU discipline felt they were being advocated for, fostering staff enthusiasm for early mobility. The fact that participants saw the makeup of the PICU care team reflected in the core PICU Up! leadership team facilitated interprofessional collaboration, as program goals were based on each discipline’s strengths.

#### Starting Small with Mobility.

Participants commented on the importance of appropriate patient selection for the first mobilization attempt. Choosing a minimally complex index patient maximized the likelihood of success and built momentum for early mobility. Generating provider comfort with mobility further drove the progressive scaling of target patient populations. “Start small and then think big. Maybe get the ambulatory children out of bed first; do not just go straight to the intubated child.”– PT

#### Sharing Successes and Evidence.

Sharing successful mobilization sessions positively influenced staff attitudes toward the PICU Up! program. Participants across all disciplines described how pictures and videos of children being mobilized built interest in PICU Up!. This visual feedback was compelling, especially when combined with patient safety data and anecdotal evidence of clinical benefits. Seeing PICU Up! in action motivated many staff members to consider mobility for their own patients. “We can talk about it, but the ability to see it with your own eyes and the impact that it has speaks louder than words.”– MD

#### Clearly Defined Protocol.

Most participants indicated that the presence of a structured leveling system with mobility inclusion criteria was beneficial, especially for those who did not have prior experience mobilizing patients. “It makes people feel more comfortable: when there are some guidelines, they know what they should be doing in certain stages for safe mobility.”– PT

#### Generating Staff Buy-In.

Bringing staff on board with program goals was critical for PICU Up! integration. Though all participants were generally supportive of early mobility, RNs, RTs, PTs, and OTs described the necessity of first consulting with front-line providers whose workflow would be most affected. Individuals on the leadership team worked closely with skeptics to create solutions that addressed patient safety and balanced early mobility with existing provider responsibilities.

#### Family Member and Caregiver Engagement.

Across disciplines, participants agreed that involving family members who were comfortable with mobilization was instrumental to the success of PICU Up!. Family participation, when appropriate, built patient trust and buy-in while empowering families with the ability to influence their child’s care in the PICU. “[Family engagement] is imperative. It brings about awareness that it does take more than just the patient. There is a sense of accomplishment…[families] feel like they are contributing to their child’s wellness.”– NP PTs and RNs further described how families promoted continuity of mobilization, as they could orient staff across different shifts to mobility activities their child responded to.

### Staff Perceptions of PICU Up!

Two distinct groups of perceptions emerged that continue to influence PICU Up! sustainability: 1) Positive Impressions and 2) Barriers and Challenges.

#### Positive Impressions

#### Patient and Family Satisfaction.

Participants stated that almost all patients and family members responded with excitement after mobilization. Most patients and families saw early mobility as a sign of progress and consequently a source of motivation. “You have kids who feel like they are moving forward – kids who talk about feeling like they are doing something toward their recovery.”– MD PTs, RNs, and NPs relayed the apprehension some families felt when mobility was initially suggested. However, apprehension often turned into enthusiasm once they witnessed their child’s response to mobilization. “That initial fear is there for some parents that ‘my kid is sick; they can’t get out of bed.’ But then after the whole process is done, parents usually say ‘I’m really glad we did this’…they can see a bit of hope.”– PT

#### Improved Morale in the PICU.

The excitement from patients and families carried over to staff. Participants reflected on the emotional encouragement of cheering on a mobilized patient and the rewarding feeling of taking care of a child as a whole. Along with effects at the individual level, staff with pre-PICU Up! experience at JHH described the unifying nature of early mobility for the interprofessional team. “There are a great deal of benefits for the [interprofessional] team in that the variety of what we are able to do has increased substantially: I’ve seen a lot of joy from other staff, including RNs and RTs, when we have taken patients for a walk for the first time.”– PT

#### Barriers and Challenges

#### Patient Safety.

Participants revealed a range of patient safety concerns, including unplanned extubations, falls, and decompensation when out of bed. Those with pre-PICU Up! experience described how the fear of adverse patient outcomes drove pushback during the initial program rollout. Patient safety still remains a concern, as frequently mentioned by non-PT/OT participants. However, with the growth of the PICU Up! program, the nature of these concerns shifted to focus on the risks of mobilizing more medically complex patients (e.g., those who were intubated or on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation).

#### Inconsistency with the Mobility Plan.

PTs, OTs, and RNs outlined how poor carryover of mobility plans between staff shifts prevented mobilization. Miscommunication of patient-specific mobility activities across staff who possessed different levels of experience often led to fragmented mobility attempts. “I was the only member who had been there from the previous day who knew what the patient should look like in the chair – so it was much more awkward, more time consuming.”– RN Participants stated that this inconsistency became a frustrating experience for both patients and family members, especially as patients stopped receiving follow-up with therapy services after transitioning to the inpatient unit floor.

#### Availability of Resources.

Staff praised the resources provided to facilitate PICU Up! implementation, but challenges in staffing and equipment management have hampered the growth of early mobility. Participants commented on the difficulty of coordinating staff schedules and priorities to mobilize a patient. Even when sufficient personnel were present, equipment designed specifically for pediatric early mobility was still limited. “I really believe that chairs and positioning devices are the biggest resources we lack.”– PT Given the lack of adequate storage space, equipment was distributed across PICU and PT/OT closets, making it difficult for staff to locate devices and determine what resources were available when a patient was ready for mobility.

#### Differences in Approaches to Sedation.

Participants described how PICU Up! implementation brought scrutiny to patient sedation, with an emphasis on safely minimizing opioid and benzodiazepine use and integrating nonpharmacologic methods of pain management. While participants acknowledged the use of the SBS to optimize sedation, a majority stated that sedation goals were still subjective and clinician-dependent. Variability in over- or under-sedating patients led to safety concerns as well as inconsistent mobility attempts. “Some kids do not get sedated enough and then other kids we are too good at over-sedating. I do not know that we have found that happy medium for what each patient needs.”– RN

#### Heterogeneity in Patient Developmental Levels.

The clinical and developmental ranges of patients in the PICU presented unique challenges for early mobility. PTs and OTs focused on difficulties with mobilizing infants and toddlers younger than 4 years old, as PICU mobilization activities that facilitate motor development in these populations are poorly defined. Participants also described the difficulty with mobilizing teenage patients, given their greater resistance to mobility and the number of staff members required to safely maneuver them.

### Improvements in Program Integration

Staff identified three improvements to better promote PICU Up! program integration.

#### Communication Between Care Teams.

RNs discussed refinements in communication of mobility plans between day and night PICU staff shifts. Many RNs who work night shifts commented on the lack of discussion about mobility that was completed throughout the day. These participants, along with SLP, indicated a desire to play a more active role in optimizing PICU Up! goals for certain patients. “I work nights…but if the child’s only been up once today, we can work on getting them moving or out of bed before bedtime.”– RN Many participants suggested that pictures, videos, and diagrams could improve communication. Visual references could help a new care team understand the mobility activities previously performed with each patient. “I tend to take pictures of the type of positioning and post them in the room. I also document it in my notes…I try to do multiple things to help [communicate].”– OT

#### Simulation of Mobility.

Pediatric mobilization simulations would allow staff to gain confidence in safely moving patients, as well as any connected lines, tubes, and drains. Participants stated that hands-on training could build competencies with particular mobility activities and assist them in developing emergency plans in case of an adverse patient event. “It would be great to partner with the simulation center and get nurses basic training to think about how to move a patient and what considerations to have, so that when you get to the clinical environment, it is a little less threatening.”– RN

#### Accessible Documentation of Mobility Goals.

Participants emphasized the need to have mobility goals documented in an accessible way. RNs, NPs, and MDs suggested adding mobility goals on whiteboards in patient rooms or in the first set of daily nursing notes to ensure that the medical team can plan appropriately. Additionally, RNs and NPs believed that the PICU Up! protocol would benefit from more clearly defined mobility goals – ones that combined existing mobility levels with developmentally appropriate activities for patients.

## DISCUSSION

We examined the long-term staff perceptions of a PICU early mobilization initiative across multiple domains, including program integration, staff perceptions, and areas of improvement. Overall, 3 years after implementation, PICU Up! continues to be well-received across each stakeholder group in the PICU. Patients and family members were perceived to play an important role in driving this enthusiasm, congruent with evidence that families perceive physical, emotional, and psychological benefits with early mobility (28, 29). The impact of PICU Up! also extended to staff, positively influencing personal role satisfaction and the interprofessional ICU team dynamic. These findings provide important insights for all interprofessional teams implementing early mobilization programs in the critical care setting.

Several themes addressed the process through which PICU Up! became embedded in unit culture. As seen with similarly structured adult and pediatric early mobility initiatives, a consistent focus on staff buy-in and interprofessional leadership remained important (28, 30, 31). Family engagement was especially critical for successful program implementation. Family members advocated for their child’s care plan and acted as an extension of the medical team to ensure mobility was not overlooked. Coupled with this, participants emphasized the need for a deliberately planned and phased program rollout. Carefully selecting an index patient to mobilize and protocolizing inclusion criteria were the first steps toward building PICU staff engagement. Novel digital strategies to disseminate evidence, anecdotes, and images emerged as previously undescribed facilitators that helped PICU Up! grow past these index cases. Consistent adoption of PICU Up! was also dependent on a bundled approach to early mobility. Participants recognized that mobilization was closely linked with sedation management, sleep hygiene improvement, delirium assessment, and daily routine normalization, all integral parts of the ICU liberation initiative (24). Incorporating multiple criteria from the ABCDEF bundle was vital for program execution, as it helped PICU Up! reach a larger patient population.

However, our results revealed barriers that still prevent provider participation and PICU Up! expansion. Resource constraints, including insufficient staff and equipment to mobilize patients, continue to challenge early mobility efforts (28, 31, 32). Although RNs, PTs, and OTs have the greatest hands-on involvement with mobility, SLP, child life, and overnight provider roles within the context of PICU Up! could be optimized. Distributing responsibility for certain mobility interventions and sleep hygiene management across the medical team could help address staffing demands. Patient safety during mobilization also remained a pressing issue. The growth of PICU Up! broadened the inclusion criteria for patients being considered for mobility, but was accompanied by an evolution in safety concerns, especially for more medically complex patients. It is clear that the recurring challenges of resource constraints and patient safety require new solutions, such as simulation of mobility scenarios – a tool that could build provider comfort, independence, and confidence with mobility.

Another important barrier was inconsistency of early mobility plans. Continuity of mobility was impacted by sedation decisions. Although goal-directed sedation using the SBS tool was integrated into the JHH PICU, staff described subjective variability and sudden changes in a patient’s sedation status that delayed mobility. Additionally, poor communication surrounding a patient’s mobility history and goals further increased uncertainty and anxiety for families as they navigated different early mobility expectations (33). To promote continuity, mobility-related communication must be stressed both within and between interprofessional teams.

While providers routinely included early mobility in their plan of care, applying PICU Up! across a heterogeneous patient population presented an ongoing challenge. Developmentally appropriate mobilization options for infants and toddlers remain unclear. The consequences are apparent, as children younger than 3 years old are less likely to receive physical rehabilitation in United States PICUs (34). At the other end of the developmental spectrum, mobilizing teenage patients posed difficulties, as it required coordination of more staff members. These findings demonstrate a need to better define feasible mobilization plans for these groups of patients. Including such interventions in the existing PICU Up! protocol may enable non-rehabilitation staff to more readily consider structured mobility for all of their patients.

Taken together, this qualitative analysis suggests that the structured, interprofessional, early mobilization program PICU Up! can be sustained at JHH. Effective implementation and broad stakeholder engagement have created a program that continues to drive enthusiasm across our PICU. The shifting barriers to mobilization highlight the importance of an interprofessional mobility team that tracks the culture surrounding mobility, evaluates emerging challenges, and develops program improvements. As we explored a multifaceted, interprofessional initiative across a wide PICU patient population, these results may have broad relevance to complex unit-level pediatric critical care interventions.

Our assessment had several potential limitations, some of which are inherent to qualitative research (35). Though purposive sampling was used, the results are based on participant data from a single tertiary-care PICU, limiting the generalizability of our findings. Participants were also unable to validate their interview transcripts or provide feedback on study findings throughout the thematic analysis process. Direct interviews with patients and family members, with interview interpretation confirmation, are necessary to further assess their perceptions of the PICU Up! program. In addition, the structured interview conditions may have resulted in participant response bias. Staff members specifically interested in early mobility may also have been the most enthusiastic to participate. We took steps to minimize the effect of social desirability and visual cues by enlisting an individual unaffiliated with the JHH PICU to conduct all interviews by phone. While telephone interviews proved advantageous to reach staff working on different professional schedules, in-person interviews could have more comprehensively considered non-verbal cues. Nevertheless, a qualitative framework proved advantageous to capture the impact of PICU Up! on staff, patients, and families beyond quantitative metrics.

## CONCLUSIONS

A structured, interprofessional, early mobilization initiative can be integrated and sustained in the PICU environment with staff, patient, and family support. PICU Up! deployment was facilitated through a defined protocol and broad stakeholder engagement that focused on cultural change in PICU practices to positively influence mobility. Barriers to program success were present during the implementation process and continue to evolve, specifically related to resource allocation, sedation management, and developmentally appropriate mobility. Individual PICUs should plan to address these challenges using institutional strengths to maximize success of early mobility initiatives.
